newsitem.title: USA: Conn. lawmakers reach budget deal at last minute.
newsitem.headline: Conn. lawmakers reach budget deal at last minute.

text.p: Connecticut lawmakers approved a $21.1 billion two-year budget just before the 1997 legislative session ended at midnight Wednesday, the Hartford Courant reported on Thursday.
The budget provides nearly $400 million in income, property and gasoline tax cuts.

The 11th-hour deal includes an extra $34 million in tax cuts, including $27 million in income tax cuts that Gov. John Rowland (R) had wanted and $7 million in additional property tax cuts that the Democrats had wanted.
The cuts were in addition to a reduction in the state's gasoline tax by 6 cents a gallon over two years.
Rowland and Democrats had wrangled over the budget for the past two weeks, and there was some doubt that an agreement would be reached before time expired.
Rowland said he will sign the two-year budget, and said the legislature will hold a short, special session in mid-June to pass the bills that could not be debated when time ran out.

The main sticking point towards the end was privatization of the state's computer operations. State employee unions had strongly opposed the privatization, fearing they could lose up to 1,000 jobs that could be shifted to big companies.
Under the agreement, the state will hire a private company to provide data processing and storage services, along with updating and integrating the system.
This will cost about $1 billion over five years, and will be the biggest government contract ever in the state.
The legislature will have veto power over the plan with a 60 percent super majority in either house.
In another controversial issue, the state moved to save $200 million over two years by adopting an early retirement program for its 50,000 employees.
The incentive-driven program is for employees who are at least 52. About 8,500 employees are eligible, and estimates are that 3,300 will take the deal.
Democrats had wanted a no-layoff provision in case not enough workers signed up. Under the agreement, the governor will get layoff rights, but only in a financial crisis.
